title: Degree adverbs and focus adverbs
subtitle: I much enjoyed / too hot / only my mother
summary: Use degree adverbs such as much and very much, keep very and too apart, and place even and only where you mean them.

lesson.heading: Degree adverbs
lesson.text: Degree adverbs go before adjectives, verbs or other adverbs to say something about the extent or level of something. Some (almost, largely, really, virtually) usually come before the main verb; others (altogether, enormously, somewhat, tremendously) usually come after it. Degree adverbs are rarely used in front position.

lesson.heading: Two jobs a focus adverb can do

left.label: Making what we say more specific
left.text: especially, even, mainly, mostly, particularly, specifically
examples: There is likely to be snow today, **particularly** in the north.
Every penny helps, and **even** the smallest donation can make a vital difference.

right.label: Limiting what we say to one thing or person
examples: Many people offered to help me invest the money, but I **only** trusted Rick.
**Only** Louis knew where the keys were kept, and nobody else.

lesson.heading: much before a verb
lesson.text: In affirmative sentences in formal contexts, **much** can be used as a degree adverb before the verbs *admire, appreciate, enjoy, prefer* and *regret*, to emphasise how we feel about something. It is used like this particularly after I and we.

examples.text: I **much enjoyed** having you stay with us.

lesson.note: We don't usually use this pattern in questions: not ~~Did you much enjoy ...?~~

left.label: much or very much
examples: I **much prefer** seeing films at the cinema than on DVD.

right.label: very much only
right.text: agree, doubt, fear, hope, like, want
examples: We **very much agree** with the decision.
or We agree very much ...; but not ~~We much agree ...~~

lesson.heading: much and very much before participles
lesson.text: Before a past participle that is part of a passive, both **much** and **very much** are possible. Before a past participle *adjective* we can use very much but not much. Before a present participle adjective we use neither.

examples.text: The new by-pass was **(very) much needed**.
I was **very much surprised** by her news.
examples.wrong: I was much surprised by her news
The hotel was very much welcoming

lesson.note: In negative sentences in informal contexts, (very) much can go before appreciate, enjoy, like and look forward to: I didn't (very) much enjoy the film.

lesson.heading: very or too?

left.label: very = to a high degree
examples: The weather was **very** hot in Majorca - perfect for swimming.
He revised **very** hard and did well in his exams.

right.label: too = more than enough, more than is wanted or needed
examples: It's **too** hot to stay in this room - let's find somewhere cooler.
The old bridge was **too** narrow for the coach to drive across.

lesson.note: In negative sentences in informal spoken English, not too can mean 'not very': I'm not too bothered about who wins.

lesson.heading: even and only: where you put them is what you mean
lesson.text: Even and only usually go in mid position, but if they refer to the subject they come in front of it - and the meaning changes.

examples.text: My mother has **only** brought some food.
**Only my mother** has brought some food.

examples.note: = in addition to everything else she can do
= you might not expect her to

lesson.text: Before a participle, ask what kind it is: passive (*much needed*), a past participle adjective (*very much surprised*, never *much surprised*), or a present participle adjective (*very welcoming*, never *very much welcoming*).

exercises.prompt: Leo was in a wheelchair as he was still ___ weak to walk far.
exercises.explanation: Too = more than is wanted: he was so weak that walking far was impossible.

exercises.prompt: We ___ hope that the striking workers will now resume negotiations.
exercises.explanation: Hope belongs to the group that takes very much only, never much on its own.

exercises.prompt: It was ___ thrilling to get Marie's news.
exercises.explanation: Thrilling is a present participle adjective, so neither much nor very much is possible.

exercises.prompt: I would ___ prefer to be remembered as kind rather than wealthy.
exercises.explanation: Prefer is one of the verbs (with admire, appreciate, enjoy, regret) that takes either much or very much.

exercises.prompt: Thanks for organising the quiz night. Your help was ___ appreciated.
exercises.explanation: This is a passive past participle, so much and very much are both fine.

exercises.statement: I was much surprised by her news.
exercises.explanation: I was very much surprised by her news. Much on its own is not used before a past participle adjective.

exercises.prompt: Kristof says that he wants to go into politics, but I ___ doubt that he's serious.
exercises.explanation: Doubt takes very much, like agree, fear, hope, like and want.

exercises.prompt: It was snowing ___ heavily for us to climb further up the mountain.
exercises.explanation: Too + adverb + for ... to means 'more than was possible'.

exercises.prompt: Ellie has agreed to start work earlier, but she's not ___ enthusiastic about it.
exercises.explanation: Both work: in informal speech not too means much the same as not very.

exercises.prompt: ___ Louis knew where the keys were kept, and nobody else.
exercises.explanation: The focus adverb refers to the subject, so it comes in front of it.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence with what it means.

pairs.left: My mother has only brought some food.
Only my mother has brought some food.
pairs.right: My mother and nobody else has brought any.
That is one more thing she can do, on top of everything else.
You might not expect her to be able to.

exercises.prompt: Does the focus adverb make what we say more specific, or limit it to one thing or person?
categories: Limits it to one thing or person
